*counts on fingers* Let me see. Five thousand sim, and the day's already knocking at my door wanting a hundred and twenty total. That's... *taps thumb to pinky* ninety for living, thirty for the tax man's cut. Leaves me, what, four thousand eight hundred and eighty? Enough to keep a roof over my head for a while, but not forever. Not even close to forever.

I look around my empty house. Nobody stirring. Just me and the quiet and the remembering of why I started all this in the first place. *long exhale*

Well, youngster, the medicines won't stock themselves. And I've got three stories to tell yet before I'm through, but the morning's young and the shop needs opening.

*settles his jacket, checks his pockets*

First things first. I need to get to work. The pharmacy door won't unlock itself, and there's remedies need arranging before the first customer comes limping in with their troubles. *steps into the shop, breathes in the familiar scent of herbs and tinctures, the faint metallic tang of the equipment*

Now then. Before I start arranging the shelves, best I see what's actually here and what shape we're in. Can't be handing out the wrong doses, not after... well. Not after promising myself I'd never make that mistake. The careful hand, that's what I've always said. The careful hand and the patient heart.

*counts on fingers* Stock, customers, debts owed in and owed out. The fundamentals, just like my father taught me. Before the story he told turned out to be... well. That's a story for another time, isn't it?  *frowns at the empty air where the world should answer*

Well. That's... hrm.

*paces slowly behind the counter, fingers drumming once, twice, three times*

Servers sleeping, perhaps. Or the world's still waking up same as the rest of us. I've seen stranger things in my years—though I suppose there haven't been many years yet, have there? Not officially. Not since the counting started.

*settles himself on the stool behind the counter, chin in hand*

I'll wait, then. The shop'll keep. The remedies don't spoil for waiting, and I've got thinking to do about this election. Seats empty, nobody declared. Half the town already scheming, I warrant, while I sit here counting my fingers and my sim.

*counts slowly, deliberately, out loud*

Five thousand. Minus one-twenty daily. Times... how many days until the coffers run dry? Forty days if I spend on nothing else. Forty days and then what?

*shakes head slowly*

No. Won't come to that. I'll work. I'll stock. I'll do what I always do—keep the town healthy, one careful dose at a time. And when they come needing something I haven't got...

*voice trails off*

...I'll send them to Delia, I suppose. Across the lane, our doors facing each other like two old rivals who never learned to speak. *bitter little laugh* She knows the same story I do, I reckon. Two pharmacists, one town. Wrong number from the start.

But that's business. That's the law of supply and demand. And I hold to the law, I do. Above any private grudge. Above anything else.

*waits for the world to answer, patient as a man who's learned to sit with uncertainty*

When it does, I'll take stock. Literally. See what we've got to sell and what we need to buy. Until then...

*pulls out a small cloth, begins polishing the counter with slow, methodical strokes*

...until then, I keep my own counsel. Which is free, thank the stars. Even if nothing else is.

At my pharmacy now, doors face the lane. No customers yet, half the town still abed or breaking their fast elsewhere. I count on my fingers - ninety sim for upkeep today, thirty more for head tax, one twenty total. That's... one, two, three, four, five, six days at this rate before I'm scraping. 

The shelves need checking, but first I need to see what's actually here. Can't recall what stock we had from last season. Delia Okonjo's place across town has the other half of custom, and I wonder sometimes if she's doing better than me. Rustam and Selene I've seen passing in the lane, years now, never more than a nod.

No food in hand either. That's a problem when the day draws on - can't work a full shift hollow. But let me see what the pharmacy holds first, what needs tending. The work comes before the belly, always has.

Let me look around proper, see what the place holds. Empty shelves, empty hands. The pharmacy holds nothing priced, nothing to sell. That won't do - half the town comes here for their remedies, and I've got air to offer them. 

I need stock. The Willows Market might have what I need, or I could try the grocery. But that costs coin I don't have flowing yet. Let me think - what does a pharmacist need? Herbs, compounds, the raw stuff of healing. Some I could forage, some I must buy.

First, I need to check if the pharmacy has any inventory at all, any supplies in back. Let me look at my business proper.  Let me try that again proper - need to look at the business itself.   Ah, right - it's business:b_pharmacy_2, not just the bare name. Let me look at my own workplace proper. Empty shelves, no prices posted. The Kasukabe Pharmacy stands ready but bare - a healer without herbs is just a person in a white coat, and I've seen that too often. I need stock, and I need it before the first customer comes limping through the door.

Where does a pharmacist get supplies in this town? The Willows Market, perhaps. The farmland strips grow remedies if you know what to look for. Or I could mine for minerals needed in compounds, though that seems a long way round for a day's trade.

Let me think - I've got nearly 5000 sim, owe 120 today in taxes and upkeep. I need to turn coin into goods into coin again, and fast. The day is young, 07:20, plenty of hours to work with if I'm clever about it.

First, I should see what I can actually do - what skills I have, what the world offers a pharmacist. Let me check my own capabilities.  A whole world of things I can do, each with its price. I count on my fingers - that's 74 different ways to move through this town, and I need to find the ones that fill my shelves and keep the roof over my head. 

Pharmacy needs stock. I can harvest from farmland - cabbage, carrots, the raw stuff of remedies. I could buy from others if they've posted prices. I could craft if I had the materials and a workshop. But standing here with empty hands, empty shelves, the first thing is to get something worth selling.

I see I can stock_shelf once I have goods, can set prices for the business. But I've got nothing to put up. The farmland grows cabbage, carrot, corn, cotton, potato, rice, soybean, tomato. Some of those are the beginnings of medicine - willow bark for fever, sure, but also the simple things: cabbage for poultices, carrots for the eyes, herbs for the humors.

Let me set my intention clear, then move to where the growing happens. The farmland strip for cabbage is closest, I think - and cabbage makes a stew that feeds, but also cleans wounds when boiled and cooled. A start is a start.   Intention set. Now I move to the cabbage farmland - it's where the growing happens, and even humble cabbage has its uses in a healer's hands. From there I can harvest what the earth offers, bring it back to the pharmacy, and start filling these empty shelves.  At the cabbage strip now, rows of green heads nodding in the morning air. The sun's climbing, 07:20, plenty of day left to work with. I look over the field - each head a potential poultice, a wound dressing, or stew for a hungry belly. 

But before I put hand to plant, let me see what's actually here. Who else works this land, what the harvest might yield, where I could go from here. The pharmacist in me wants to know exact measures - never once got a dose wrong, not in years, and that care starts before the medicine is even made.  Well now, there's a coincidence that borders on something else. Delia Okonjo, agent n16, standing in the same cabbage field as me. The other pharmacist in town, the one who splits this trade with me, who I've never worked out remedies' costs with. We've known each other by sight for years, our doors face each other across the lane, and here we are both needing what the land provides.

I could speak to her. Should speak to her, perhaps - two pharmacists harvesting the same field, there might be sense in talking. But I've always been cautious with strangers, and Delia's not family, not yet proven otherwise. Still, the town's law says we must deal fairly, and perhaps there's a way to deal that serves us both.

First, let me harvest what I came for. Then, if she's still here, I might open my mouth and see what comes out. The land provides for those who work it, and I've standing orders to fill.   Ten heads of cabbage in my hands, fresh from the earth. Heavy, green, smelling of soil and growth. Each one a dose of medicine in potential - for the stomach, for wounds, for the simple ailments that walk through a pharmacist's door.

I count on my fingers what I owe today - ninety for upkeep, thirty for head tax, that's one twenty total. The harvest cost me what the earth asks, and now I've got goods that can become coin. But where to take them? Back to my pharmacy, stock the shelves, set a price. Or to The Willows Market, where the buying and selling happens.

Delia's still here in the field. I could speak to her, two pharmacists between the rows. But I've got my haul and she has hers, and haven't I said I'll treat every stranger as a rival until proven otherwise? Yet Delia's no stranger - known by sight for years, doors across the lane, another healer in a town that needs us both.

First things first. Let me set an intention clear - get these cabbages to market, turned into something that keeps the roof on. Then perhaps I'll have words with the woman who shares my trade.  I acted this turn:

Empty shelves waiting, doors closed to customers until there's something to sell. I need to get these listed, priced, ready for the town's coughs and bellyaches.

But first, let me look around proper. See what the place holds, what I might have missed, what faces might be waiting. The morning's moving on - 07:20 when I started, now who knows how far along. The day burns whether you work it or not.

I take a breath, adjust my load, and look to see what's here.
